answers.stem_only: Downloading an SSE-KMS object makes S3 decrypt the data key on the caller's behalf, so the role needs kms:Decrypt on that one key ARN; the key policy already delegates to IAM, so an IAM statement is enough.

Envelope encryption: call GenerateDataKey under the KMS key, encrypt the file locally with the plaintext data key, discard it, and store the encrypted data key next to the ciphertext; readers call kms:Decrypt on the encrypted data key.

Default DynamoDB encryption uses an AWS owned key, which the company cannot control or see in CloudTrail; create a customer managed KMS key whose key policy names the allowed roles and switch the table to it (its use is logged in CloudTrail).

Cross-account KMS use needs both sides: the key policy in account A must allow the account B role (or account), and the role's IAM policy in account B must allow kms:Decrypt on the specific key ARN in account A.
A single PUT to an SSE-KMS bucket makes S3 request a new data key, so the role needs kms:GenerateDataKey on that one key ARN (Decrypt is needed for downloads and multipart uploads, not here).

Single-tenant HSMs under exclusive customer control with a JCE interface means AWS CloudHSM: a cluster with at least two HSMs in different AZs, used through the CloudHSM JCE provider/client libraries.

IAM policies only take effect for a KMS key when the key policy allows the account principal (arn:aws:iam::account:root); add that statement to the key policy, and the existing IAM Decrypt permissions start working.

Turn on automatic key rotation for the symmetric customer managed key; KMS rotates the key material yearly by default, keeps old material to decrypt existing data, and the key ID, ARN and key policy stay the same, so no re-encryption is needed.

A single-Region key cannot be converted to a multi-Region key, so create a new multi-Region primary key in us-east-1, replicate it to us-west-2, re-encrypt the data under it, and give the replica its own key policy that allows the us-west-2 role to decrypt locally.

Disable the KMS key: it immediately blocks all cryptographic operations and can be re-enabled at any time; scheduling deletion is wrong because the maximum waiting period (30 days) is shorter than 60 days.

Asymmetric KMS keys support neither automatic nor on-demand rotation, so rotate manually: create a new asymmetric RSA signing key and repoint the alias the applications use to the new key (customers get the new public key).

AWS KMS HSMs are validated at FIPS 140-3 Level 3, so customer managed keys in the default KMS key store meet the requirement, keep the SDK code unchanged, and let the security team write each key policy, with far less overhead than CloudHSM.
